# Game Night Discord Activity

An independently packaged Discord Activity for Unnamed Tracking App. It uses
Plugin API **v1.1.12** public-app infrastructure and the updated Discord Bot
Notifications identity adapter. It imports no host modules and has no database,
network sockets, bot token or OAuth client secret of its own.

The signed **0.2.1** release is available from the official plugin catalogue under
**Unnamed Tracking Official**. Updates require manual review. This is an early
release; pricing, federation and the remaining device/context acceptance work
are documented limitations, not implied by its signature.

## What works

- Verified Discord OAuth identity and live Activity instance membership.
- Shared persisted rooms, individual inputs, host transfer and reconnect recovery.
- User-approved connections to independent HTTPS tracking instances.
- Guest games and explicit self-reported multiplayer compatibility annotations.
- Strict, balanced and discovery modes, personal hard platform/genre/time rules.
- A shortlist of up to three games, one vote per participant, personal vetoes,
  selection and rerolls. Ties use a random draw among tied eligible games.
- Imported cover artwork where available, readable fallbacks, eligibility reasons.
- Public Steam cover fallback and title details with Steam/own tracking-page links.
- Verified Discord avatars and circular participant thumbnails.
- Saved group-play presets from connected libraries, with manual confirmation for
  unknown multiplayer counts; entry-specific genres reset after adding a game.
- Room-host matching settings, personal undo-veto controls, and spectators for
  participants with no games. Host transfer requires a separate confirmation.
- Native Discord invitation controls and optional verified DM/group-DM rooms.
- Automatic owned multiplayer contributions; one participant can supply missing
  player limits for the room directly from the exclusion list. Saved/manual
  limits also supply missing counts without repeated entry. Personal access,
  known platform-specific limits, rules and crossplay consent remain separate.
- Optional room limits can be saved independently. An unknown minimum stays
  unknown while the maximum is retained (and vice versa). Saving a partial range
  confirms only the current group size; changed groups need approval again and
  still cannot exceed a known bound. Complete ranges remain reusable.
- Native library bulk multiplayer presets and optional cross-instance saves under
  separate `compatibility.write` consent, with per-game failure results.
- Own-account tracking changes and explicitly local achievement reports when the
  participant grants the appropriate write scopes.
- Responsive layout, keyboard controls and reduced-motion support.

Current purchase offers are unavailable in the host. Price, budget and discount
filters are paused. Strict still requires everyone to own the game; balanced and
discovery allow a participant to consider an unowned game only with their own
purchase consent and owned-only rule disabled. Unknown prices are labeled and
never reported as free or within budget. No action authorizes a purchase.
Wishlist entries are never treated as ownership. Compatibility annotations are
self-reported, not provider verification; title matches need edition confirmation.

## Configure

1. Install **Discord Bot Notifications** and **Game Night** from the official
   catalogue in Administration → Plugins. Review their verified publisher,
   compatibility and permissions. For an unpublished branch build, use its separate
   unsigned-development package review instead.
2. Grant the Activity `integrations.public_app` and `plugin.storage` globally.
   Grant the bot `integrations.identity_provider` explicitly, alongside its existing
   permissions. Neither grant is implied by `api.full`.
3. Configure the bot token/server using the bot administrator page. Add the same
   application's ID and OAuth client secret under **Discord Activity sign-in**.
   Existing notification destinations retain their configuration and proof.
4. Enable integration access on the Activity host. Enable guests if desired.
5. Configure Discord Activity URL mappings:
   `/` → `HOST/api/public-apps/official.discord-social-activity/app/`
   and `/api` → `HOST/api`. Enable Activities for the tested platforms. Keep a
   redirect URI configured for the Embedded App SDK OAuth flow.
6. On each source instance, enable integrations and approve the Activity host's
   exact HTTPS origin. Participants sign in on that source and approve their own
   scopes/expiry; write scopes default to unchecked.
7. Launch from the Discord App Launcher in the bot's configured server. Connect
   an instance or add manual games, confirm compatibility, then shortlist and vote.

For private-channel rooms, explicitly enable **Allow Activities in DMs and group
DMs** in the bot's Activity settings. Discord must also allow user installation
and private-channel launch for your application/testers. The adapter validates
Discord's `pc` location and connected user list; enabling DMs does not allow
Activities in other guilds. See the complete
[operator/player setup guide](../../wiki/docs/examples/discord-game-night.md).

Public sessions are separate external principals, not host accounts. Credentials
for connected instances remain encrypted in the host broker, and never enter this
plugin or the browser. Removing a source connection forgets its broker credential;
revoke it in the source instance's Connected apps to invalidate the grant there too.

Users may explicitly choose **Until revoked** instead of timed access. Remembered
links belong to the verified Discord identity and are reused on reconnect while
their credentials remain valid. The first connection always needs consent; a
Discord username or display name alone never links an application account.

For an older source without the delegation API, the Activity operator can enable
**Allow unsafe legacy API-key connections** in Integration access. The participant
must select legacy mode and acknowledge the broad key. The host encrypts it and
uses only fixed identity/library GET requests. Legacy connections cannot write
tracking, achievements or multiplayer settings and do not expose imported artwork; public Steam cover
fallback still applies. Disconnect the connection and revoke the key on the old
instance when finished. Legacy clients do not require upgrading the old instance.

Source administrators may optionally allow consent requests from any HTTPS origin.
Library connections request only identity and game reads by default. Participants
can choose optional progress access before connecting; the source still presents
tracking and achievement writes unchecked for explicit approval. Unused history,
media and custom-list capabilities are not requested by Game Night.
This registers requesters without individual origin setup; it never approves a
user's data. Individually disabled origins stay blocked. Central Activity hosting
can connect independent source instances through this same broker and consent
boundary. Operator approval, personal rules and personal vetoes remain distinct.

Game titles use normalized case, spacing and punctuation by default. Copies a
participant grouped as one game on their instance (for example *Minecraft for
Windows* under *Minecraft*, from the library's `identity.main_title`) match by that
game's main title. Steam IDs are optional; edition ambiguity still requires human
confirmation. Platform
aliases and empty-library spectators can be configured by the current room host.
For one or two players, detected multiplayer is accepted with unknown limits. Larger groups can approve games without extra details for the current player count, or set known limits once. Known constraints still win. Steam app IDs infer PC only when the platform is blank. Both shortcuts are configurable by the room host.
Store metadata is informational and cannot override personal rules.

## Build and test

Administrators can use **Game Night participants** in Administration to inspect
saved names/IDs and source states, unlink connections, or purge participant/all
local Activity data with confirmation. Updating requires reviewing the separate
`integrations.public_app.admin` and native admin-page permissions. Host enforcement
checks the administrator and exact installation; public participants cannot use
this API. Room cleanup clears cached results as well as participant inputs.
Source libraries and upstream grants are not deleted. Guest/room retention can
be set to365 days; valid remembered source grants have their own lifetime.
Connected apps shows the external account label; older remote grants need fresh
consent. Retroactive account merging is a separate follow-up.

```sh
npm install
npm run build:activity
npm run check:activity
python -m pytest tests/test_discord_activity.py tests/test_discord_activity_identity.py
python tools/build_packages.py
```

Source is under `ui/`; compiled assets are under `frontend/` and included in the
validated `.utp`. The builder preserves historical published packages. Test the
actual preview package against the matching host branch before deployment.

The Activity stores bounded room inputs/votes using public storage CAS. Rooms
expire under the host retention policy; its background worker clears expired
rooms. Temporary host-gateway outages retry with delays from one to thirty seconds;
permission denials and other permanent failures remain visible in Diagnostics.
For a blank or refused Activity, follow the [operator troubleshooting steps](../../wiki/docs/examples/discord-game-night.md#troubleshooting)
to distinguish a failed worker from a reverse-proxy frame header or OAuth problem.
There is no persistent Discord Gateway connection, custom chat command or
notification delivery in the Activity. Those remain the bot's responsibilities.

The [architecture and acceptance matrix](../../wiki/docs/architecture/discord-game-night.md) links the implementation to the open issues and distinguishes verified behavior from release follow-ups.

# Epic Games Library

Optional personal Epic game imports through **Plugin API 1.1.19**. Requires a host
that implements `games.import` with artwork addresses, connection sync actions and
personal scheduled tasks. Older hosts reject this package during compatibility review;
use an earlier Epic release on a host that predates 1.1.19. This plugin uses the existing SDK v1.1.1 wire helper.
The host page/sign-in support is completed by
[host PR40](https://github.com/Unbound-Timeline-Shelf/Unbound-Timeline-Shelf/pull/40).

## Experimental service dependency

Epic does not publish or support an API for third-party library imports, and
this plugin is not affiliated with or endorsed by Epic Games. It does not use
Epic Online Services or Epic Account Services, and Unnamed Tracking App has no
Epic-issued OAuth client. Instead, the plugin signs in the same way the Epic
Games Launcher does: Epic's own sign-in page returns a one-time authorization
code for the launcher's public client, and the plugin exchanges that code for
launcher access/refresh tokens. It then reads the same unofficial account,
library, playtime and catalogue services the launcher uses.

Those services are undocumented and Epic can change, rate-limit or withdraw them
at any time. Treat the integration as experimental: an Epic-side change can stop
sign-in, imports or playtime until a new plugin release adapts to it. Epic
support cannot help with this plugin; report problems to this repository instead
(see [Troubleshooting and support](#troubleshooting-and-support)).

An Epic service failure is not host data loss. Failed sign-ins, refreshes,
inventory pages, playtime or catalogue lookups stop the current step and keep
your saved connection, checkpoint and library. The plugin never deletes games.
Disconnecting removes only this plugin's saved tokens and checkpoint for your
account; imported games, notes, ratings, status and playtime stay in the host.

## Imported fields

Each Epic game is imported with its title and its Epic identity (catalogue
namespace and item ID, scoped to the connected account). When Epic's catalogue
supplies them, the description, developer and publisher are imported too. Total
playtime is imported when Epic's playtime service answers. Catalogue text is
requested in US English.

Artwork is sent as addresses only; the host downloads, checks and resizes the
pictures itself and fills only pictures the game does not already have, so an
upload of yours or earlier artwork is never replaced. The plugin picks the best
catalogue `keyImages` entry for each field (preferred type first, then the larger
picture):

| Host field | Epic image types, best first |
| --- | --- |
| `key_art_url` | `DieselGameBoxTall`, `OfferImageTall`, `DieselStoreFrontTall` |
| `banner_url` | `DieselGameBox`, `DieselStoreFrontWide`, `OfferImageWide` |
| `logo_url` | `DieselGameBoxLogo`, `ProductLogo` |
| `icon_url` | `Thumbnail` |

Each address is checked before it is sent, using the host's rules (at most 2048
characters, `http`/`https` on port 80 or 443, no credentials, fragment or
control characters, public host only). An address that fails is dropped and the
game is still imported without that picture. If the host cannot download a
picture it reports it and the import continues; the Epic page counts these as
`artwork_failed` and the next sync offers the address again. Games that are
unavailable never send artwork.

Not imported: release dates (Epic's catalogue exposes only listing and record
timestamps such as `creationDate`, which are not the game's release date, so
sending them would overwrite correct dates), genres/tags, achievements, prices,
DLC/add-ons, ratings badges and install state. Use the host's metadata lookup for
those. The import sends only the fields the host's `games.import` contract
accepts (Plugin API 1.1.19); a test pins this so a future field cannot be added
without a host contract change. Checkpoints saved before artwork support still
resume and import normally; artwork is added on the next sync.

## Connect and import

Install this plugin's `.utp` through Settings → Plugins, approve the declared
permissions and enable it. Open Settings → Account → Connections, where **Epic Games**
is listed with its connection status. Choose **Connect** (or **Manage** once
connected) to open the plugin page in a popup. The page is also reachable at its
plugin route, but it no longer adds a sidebar entry.
The popup uses the host's appearance and spacing, with an account summary and
import controls. Expand **Use your regular browser**, then use **Copy sign-in link** to open Epic in your regular browser while leaving the
app open. If clipboard access is unavailable, copy the selected link manually.
Alternatively, use **Sign in on Epic Games**. The action is declared as external navigation, so
the host validates Epic's returned HTTPS destination and opens it in a new tab,
leaving this popup open; the sandboxed plugin does not open a popup itself.
After signing in, Epic shows a page of text. Select all of it, copy it and paste
it into the code field: pasting the whole page connects without another click.
The one-time authorization code, its JSON page, a single copied JSON line or the
redirect URL are all accepted. Hosts that predate new-tab handling, or a browser
that blocks the tab, navigate the host tab instead; then use browser Back and
reopen **Connections → Epic Games**. No popup permission is needed. Your
password stays on Epic's site. The code is cleared immediately after submission
and is never saved in settings.

If Epic later rejects the saved sign-in (for example after a password change),
the popup shows the code field again. **Replace sign-in** does the same at any
time. The existing connection stays until Epic accepts the new code; an
accepted replacement then starts a fresh import checkpoint, and games already
imported stay in your library.

Launcher access/refresh tokens are validated independently from the 32-character
account ID and bounded to 8 KiB. Hosts must support authorization headers larger
than the original 2 KiB limit; older hosts need the companion token-header fix
before an import can use these tokens. Failed replacement sign-ins retain an
existing connection and never show token values in errors.

Positive, finite access-token lifetimes from Epic are accepted, including lifetimes
longer than one day. The plugin schedules refresh at the shorter of that lifetime
and one day, so a longer provider lifetime does not delay local token rotation.
Malformed expiry values retain an existing connection.

Choose **Import games**. Inventory paging, playtime, catalogue lookup and host
imports run as separate bounded steps. **Pause after this step**, closing the
page or a failed request retains the checkpoint. **Resume import** continues it.
An import started from this popup (or from Games → **Sync / import**, which opens it)
is driven by the popup itself: closing it pauses that import at the last saved step;
nothing keeps running on the server for it. **Connections → Sync now** and the personal
autosync below run on the server instead, without the popup, and resume the same
checkpoint. Handing the popup's own Import/Resume to that server-run workflow needs a
public start/status bridge the host does not offer yet (host issue
[#466](https://github.com/Unbound-Timeline-Shelf/Unbound-Timeline-Shelf/issues/466)).
**Start new inventory** deliberately replaces the current checkpoint. Disconnect
removes this user's saved tokens/checkpoint and keeps imported games.

The popup follows Steam's host dialog sizing and shared appearance. Disconnected
accounts show sign-in controls; import controls appear after connecting.
On Games, **Sync / import → Sync Epic Games** starts or resumes the same
import flow. The menu does not add a second connection page.

For automatic imports, open **Account → Background tasks → Epic Games autosync**.
Approve the declared `tasks.background` access and enable your own schedule; it
starts off and normally runs daily. Intervals can range from 5 minutes to 1 week.
Each run advances one bounded checkpoint; incomplete work requests the next step
after 60 seconds, even with the page closed. Completion restores your chosen interval.
Disabling autosync stops queued steps. Manual and automatic imports share the same
per-user lease, tokens, checkpoint and preservation rules; another user's schedule
cannot adopt your Epic account or change your library.

Games use namespace + catalogue identity within the connected account. Similar
titles and another Epic account cannot adopt each other's games. Engine assets,
private sandboxes, DLC and digital extras are skipped. Catalogue requests group
up to 25 entries in one namespace. An entry Epic omits (for example a delisted
item) is skipped individually: it is counted in `skipped`/`catalogue_missing`, listed
in `skipped_entries` (first 25 shown) and later games continue. Transport failures or
an unreadable catalogue response still stop the step and retain the batch for retry. A repeated/invalid cursor, invalid record, incomplete page or safety
limit stops inventory before availability changes.

Successful imports respect the host's field locks, manual status, notes and
ratings. Playtime only increases; absent/unavailable playtime leaves known values
alone. When multiple launcher artifacts share a catalogue identity, the largest
reported artifact total is used to avoid counting duplicate platform entries.
Only a complete valid inventory can mark previously imported games unavailable.

## Troubleshooting and support

Messages come from the plugin and never include token values. Most Epic-side
failures are recovered by waiting and choosing **Resume import**.

| Message or symptom | What it means and what to do |
| --- | --- |
| "Paste the 32-character authorization code, its JSON page or redirect URL." | The pasted text did not contain exactly one code. Choose **Sign in on Epic Games** (or **Copy sign-in link**) again and paste the whole page Epic shows. Each code works once. |
| "Epic rejected this sign-in. Sign in on Epic again and paste a fresh code." | Epic no longer accepts the saved sign-in (for example after a password change), or rejected the pasted code. Choose **Replace sign-in** and paste a fresh code. If this happens during autosync, the schedule turns itself off; re-enable it in **Account → Background tasks** after reconnecting. |
| "Epic returned a different account. Reconnect before importing." | A token refresh answered for another Epic account. Use **Replace sign-in** with the account you intend to import. As above, re-enable autosync afterwards if it turned off. |
| "Epic is busy. Wait a minute, then resume the import." | Epic rate-limited the request. Wait, then **Resume import**. Autosync retries on its own after at least five minutes. |
| "Epic could not be reached or refused the request. Your saved import is retained." | Epic's service was unavailable or answered with an error. Resume later; the checkpoint is kept. |
| "Epic returned an incomplete inventory…", "…invalid inventory paging information", "…repeated an inventory cursor", "…omitted catalogue entries", "…omitted a game title" or "…unreadable game categories" | Epic's reply did not match what the plugin expects. Nothing is marked unavailable from a partial inventory. Resume later; if it persists across days it is probably an Epic-side change, so report it. |
| "Epic playtime was unavailable. Existing playtime was retained." | Games still import; known playtime is not lowered or cleared. A later import fills playtime when Epic answers again. |
| "Another Epic action is running. Wait briefly, then resume." | Two Epic actions for your account overlapped, for example a manual import and autosync. Wait about a minute and resume. |
| "Start a new import for this connected account." | The saved checkpoint belongs to an earlier connection. Choose **Start new inventory**. |
| "Epic's inventory exceeded the safety limit. Availability has not changed." | The library exceeded 10,000 entries or 200 inventory pages. Report it. |
| "The host denied or could not complete this action. Check plugin permissions, then retry." | A host-side refusal, not an Epic failure. In **Settings → Plugins**, check that the plugin is enabled and its permissions are approved. |
| **Local conflicts** count increases | A game you deleted in the app, or one whose identity changed, is left alone instead of being recreated. |

Only a complete, valid inventory marks games that left your Epic library as
unavailable. They are not deleted, and they become available again when a later
import lists them.

Report persistent Epic sign-in or import failures as an
[issue in this repository](https://github.com/Unbound-Timeline-Shelf/Plugins/issues),
not to Epic or the host application. Include the plugin version (shown in
**Settings → Plugins**), the host release or image tag you deployed and the exact
message. Never include the authorization code, the text of Epic's sign-in page,
the redirect URL, tokens or your Epic account ID. Installation, permission and Connections-page problems that
are not specific to Epic belong to the host's plugin documentation.

# Jellyfin Media Sync â€” official preview

This official preview is under test, with automatic package updates disabled.
The independently installable `official.jellyfin-media-sync` package is
separate from `example.jellyfin-media-sync`, which remains a demonstration.
There is no automatic conversion of the demo's private storage or permission grants.

An administrator adds servers and discovery keys on **Jellyfin servers** directly
under **Administration → Server management** in Settings, tests them, and approves
libraries. Personal connections live at **Account → Your Jellyfin accounts** and
the direct **Media → Jellyfin** sidebar entry. These placements require separate
consent for the administration and account settings areas. Loading and failed
configuration requests show a retry control and the host's access/runtime details;
administrator denial is shown only after a successful role check.
Music, books, Live TV and collections
are excluded. Explicit film/TV/anime mappings win over automatic anime tag/genre
detection. Anime films become a one-episode anime entry; season zero is supported.

On **Jellyfin**, each user connects multiple accounts using a password or Quick
Connect. A password is used once, never persisted. Alternatively, the administrator
can approve a specific remote identity for the shared discovery key. Users can narrow
approved libraries, choose automatic sync and merging, opt into error notifications,
and order accounts for Watch Now. All enabled accounts participate in sync.
Removing a credential retains configuration, item mappings and checkpoints.
Quick Connect shows a code to approve in Jellyfin and then completes by itself: the
page checks every two seconds for as long as the code lives (five minutes), stops on
success, expiry or an error, and keeps a "Check now" button as a fallback. Every
connection signs in to Jellyfin under its own device id, so connecting or reconnecting
one account never signs another one out (Jellyfin keeps a single token per user and
device id). Sign-in problems are shown as messages on the page.
Unnumbered episodes retain provider progress and enter review. Assign their real
season/episode numbers or leave them unnumbered; the plugin never fabricates numbers
or marks a partially numbered series complete. Missing runtimes remain unknown.

Sync imports all supported items, including unwatched titles, watched episodes,
position ticks, percentage, play counts and last-played timestamps. Provider IDs
and unique exact title/year matches merge into the user's existing media records.
Ambiguous matches and local watch-state changes enter a review queue. Notes,
ratings and manually locked metadata survive enrichment. Personal ratings are
imported only where absent. Jellyfin supplies descriptions, credits, genres,
studios, countries, languages, tags, dates, codec details, provider identities and
token-free artwork URLs. Year-only dates retain their precision in provider metadata.
Authenticated-only artwork may not display; tokens are never added to image URLs.

Optional **Playback Reporting** imports real individual viewing sessions through
that Jellyfin plugin's read-only user/day API. It requires an installed, active
Playback Reporting plugin and an elevated discovery credential. Choose a bounded
initial lookback (default 30 days, up to 3650). Without it, ordinary Jellyfin cannot
reconstruct earlier sessions from its aggregate counters; the plugin reports this
limitation and never invents past plays or timestamps. No new Jellyfin-side plugin
is required. Sync never changes Jellyfin watched state, ratings, files or media.

One supervised worker processes bounded pages and saves accepted checkpoints.
Host downtime, permission denial and restarts preserve progress. Backoff is bounded
and configurable; authentication/configuration failures wait for correction.
The next automatic run replaces the previous retry schedule, with no overlapping
per-account jobs. Disabling automatic sync stops future schedules; an active run
finishes. Full rescan starts a fresh census. Two successful censuses must miss an
item before its Watch Now link becomes unavailable; personal media is retained.

HTTP and untrusted certificates produce connection-test warnings. HTTPS always
uses host CA trust; there is no certificate-verification bypass. Base URLs may
include a reverse-proxy path; redirects are refused. Secrets stay in private
`plugin.storage` broker namespaces and are never returned by configuration/status
actions. This storage is access-controlled by the runtime, not an encrypted vault;
protect runtime backups accordingly. The plugin has no host database, filesystem,
environment or secret access. Native UI keeps the existing privileged permission
and requires normal user grants. Optional notification denial does not stop sync. With the opt-in, each account has one
notification story (Plugin API 1.1.14): a sync problem opens it, a different problem revises it and a
successful sync resolves it, with a link to the accounts page; hosts or grants without story support
receive the earlier single message.

Target: the current `plugin-manager` public API and Jellyfin 12.1.0. Manifest ranges
remain `^1.0.0`; compatibility detection is intentionally deferred. Provider-neutral
media enrichment and bounded JSON POST are host API additions, available equally
to all plugins. No plugin-specific host hook or trust bypass is used.

Build a validated preview with `python tools/build_packages.py`. Packages and
catalogue previews land under `.validation/`; published historical packages remain
immutable. The 0.0.1 preview is published through the reviewed official signing
identity; automatic updates remain disabled during validation. Unsigned local packages must
use the host's normal untrusted-package approval flow. Test signing keys are for
disposable integration tests only and never confer production trust.


Requires Plugin API v1.1.17 for declared page activation. The native bundle loads
when a contributed page is opened, rather than during unrelated library navigation.
Status polls read compact state every five seconds while syncing and every thirty
seconds while idle. Hidden pages pause requests; full configuration reloads when
review counts or completed syncs change, preserving unsaved preferences.

## Watch in Jellyfin

Availability is decided at library sync. Every `media.sync` write for a matched item
carries `watch_url` (the item's deep link in the configured server's web UI, without
credentials) and `watch_label` (`Jellyfin · <server name>`, at most 80 characters)
alongside `available`. The host stores them on the media's Jellyfin source link and
renders the "Watch in <label>" button itself, so opening a media page performs no plugin
lookup. An item that disappears from two successful scans is re-sent with
`available: false` (and its link), and the host stops offering it. The plugin no longer
contributes its own panel or media menu entry to media pages.

The `watch-now` action remains as a fallback for items synced before this change. Its
results are cached per user in one `watchcache/<user>` record (64 items, 60 s found /
15 s not available). Writes to servers, accounts, profiles or credentials drop the
affected cache, a completed sync drops that user's cache, and plugin start clears all
caches. `cached_only` answers `{"ok": false, "pending": true}` on a miss without a
lookup; `refresh` evicts and looks up again.

# Atlas Metadata Provider

Search and enrich games, anime, movies and TV shows from an [Atlas](https://github.com/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata) server. Atlas can merge Steam, IGDB, TMDB and curated sources into one canonical record, while the app combines Atlas with its other providers using the user's provider ranking. Uses public Plugin API v1.1.20 (search, metadata, media, health), so it needs a host on Plugin API 1.1.20 or later: an older host refuses to install it and keeps the previous release.

## Configure

Install its .utp through Plugin Manager and grant the declared permissions, then set, in the host-rendered provider settings (system or personal scope):

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Atlas API URL** | Root used by the app server to reach your Atlas node, e.g. `https://atlas.example.org` or `http://atlas:8000` on a shared Docker network. A path prefix is allowed (`https://host/atlas`). No credentials, query or fragment. |
| **Public Atlas URL (optional)** | Root that a user's browser can reach. Leave blank when it is the same as the API URL. Set it when the app server uses an internal Docker address but Atlas is published at a different URL, such as API URL `http://atlas:8000` and public URL `https://atlas.example.org`. Artwork, achievement icons, and Atlas record links use this address. |
| **Atlas API token** | A token with the `read` scope (`atlas token --name tracker --scopes read`). Write-only and encrypted by the host. |

Use your own server, a LAN mirror or a public one; the plugin contacts only the configured URL. Egress is governed by the `network.outbound` grant, so the administrator chooses the destination.

## Behaviour

- **Search** is filtered to the requested media type and returns lightweight candidates with Atlas ID plus linked store/provider identifiers (`steam`, `igdb`, `tmdb`, ...) so the host can cross-link them.
- **Metadata** is fetched by Atlas ID. A candidate without one is resolved by linked provider IDs or exact title and year, constrained to the same media type; only certain matches are accepted (Atlas `reason` `id`, `redirect`, `crosswalk` or `exact`). A `conflict` (the candidate's identifiers point at different Atlas records), an `ambiguous` or cross-type answer and a fuzzy match are never adopted: the plugin returns no metadata, writes the conflicting Atlas IDs to its log and leaves the choice to a curator in Atlas. The year is sent as the release date (`2011`). An Atlas that predates `reason` is read as before (`method` `crosswalk` or `exact`, and no `conflict`); it cannot report conflicts, so against it a conflicting pair can still resolve to the record that owns the first identifier. Returned records include an **Atlas record** link so you can open Atlas and propose missing identifiers through its linking workflow.
- **Metadata fields** are mapped by media type to the app's provider-neutral contract. Games include developer, publisher, series, features, platforms and multiplayer facts. Movies include director, studio, runtime, writers and production countries. Anime includes studios, format, episode count and themes. TV shows include creators, episode count and episode runtime; networks and season count remain visible as provider custom details. All types can include release date, description, tags, genres, languages, alternate titles, age rating, links, scores, provider IDs and bounded Atlas custom values. Invalid or missing fields are omitted. Provider ordering in the app determines the default winner when sources disagree; fields no other provider supplies still complement the result.
- **Release dates** keep their precision (Plugin API 1.1.20, Atlas contract C5). Atlas's `first_release` is sent as `first_release` (`{"date": "2011-04", "precision": "month"}`), so a year-only or month-only release is never shown as 1 January. `release_date` stays day-only: it is sent only for a real calendar day, and a day `first_release` always names the same day. Up to five regional `releases` (date, precision, platform, region, edition, category) are forwarded in Atlas's order; an entry with an unusable value is left out, not altered. `year` comes from the first release at any precision. Against an Atlas that predates partial dates, a partial value in its legacy `release_date` key (a curator lock such as `2011`) is read as that year or month, and a free-text one (`TBA`) sends no date.
- **Relations** between games (Plugin API 1.1.20, Atlas contract C6). Atlas's own relations of a game (its `parents`, such as the base game of a DLC, the original of a remake or port, and its `members_of`, a series or collection) are sent as `relations`: `{"candidate": {"provider": "official.metadata-atlas.atlas", "external_id": <the other record's Atlas id>, "title": ..., "provider_ids": {"atlas": ...}}, "relation": "dlc_of", "group": "related"}`, ordered by relation type (the shared vocabulary order) and then Atlas id, at most 64. The host links the game to the one it tracks under that Atlas id, or keeps the reference until it does. Incoming relations (`children`, `members`) belong to the other record and travel with its refresh. Only the twelve types of the shared vocabulary are sent; any other (`edition_of`, `bundle_contains`, a future type) is left out and its name logged, and a malformed entry is skipped. Editions are not relations (C6.1): an edition reaches the host as the `edition` of a regional release. A game found through a Steam or IGDB id gets its relations too: `/resolve` does not include them, so the plugin reads the record once more. An Atlas without relations sends none.
- **Identifiers** sent to the host are bounded as the host requires (at most 32: `atlas` first, then the well-known store and catalogue namespaces such as `steam`, `igdb`, `gog`, `epic`, `rawg`, `tmdb` and `imdb`, then the others sorted, so a record whose sources claim many obscure namespaces keeps its store ids; a value that is not a string or number is left out), and `/resolve` receives only real provider namespaces within Atlas's limits (at most 32 ids of up to 256 characters; a title over 500 characters is left out). The host's library candidate also lists its own identity under its provider id (`local`, whose value is the title); that key is not sent.
- **Achievements** are game-only definitions (name, description, hidden flag, global percentage, cached icons, stable IDs and source IDs), never player progress. The host stores definitions without changing progress and can resolve them through linked IDs such as Steam. Non-game records never request the game achievement endpoint.
- **Media** lists only artwork Atlas has already downloaded and verified, as `<public-server>/media/<hash>` links. For anime, movies and TV, Atlas key art is exposed as a poster. Achievement icons use the same verified media path. The public URL must be reachable by the app's browser; keeping it separate from the API URL lets the app server use a private Docker address without exposing that address to browsers.
- Merged Atlas IDs keep working: a record merged into another (also through a chain of merges) is returned under its current ID, and metadata, artwork and achievements are read from that live record.
- **Identity** (Plugin API 1.1.20, contract C4.4): each metadata patch says how the record was found, as `identity.match` (`id` for the Atlas ID the host holds, otherwise Atlas's own `/resolve` reason: `redirect`, `crosswalk` or `exact`). When the Atlas ID the host holds was merged into another record, the patch is `{"match": "redirect", "previous_ids": {"atlas": <the held ID>}}` next to the live ID in `provider_ids`, so the host rewrites its saved ID to the live one (C4.4 rule 2) instead of keeping the merged-away ID and depending on Atlas's redirect. A `/resolve` lookup runs only when the host holds no Atlas ID, so its `redirect` carries no `previous_ids`. A record Atlas serves under another ID without a redirect is not reported as a move. A record whose `redirected_from` names an ID other than the one requested is not adopted at all (no patch, no identity), because Atlas did not say that the held ID moved. **Known limitation (unmerge):** once the host has followed a merge from A to C, an Atlas unmerge that brings A back leaves the host holding C. C is still a live record, so later refreshes match it by `id` and keep applying C's metadata; the host recovers only when a person rematches the game (the old ID stays in its field-change history). Following an unmerge back needs Atlas's change feed (C4.2 `/changes`) or an unmerge signal in the Plugin API, which neither this plugin nor the host reads yet. A conflicting or ambiguous `/resolve` answer still returns no patch (logged, as above), so `identity.match` `conflict` is not sent yet. Under an older declared contract no `identity` is sent.
- Failures are typed (`not_configured`, `invalid_configuration` for a bad URL or rejected token, `rate_limited`, `unavailable`); remote bodies and the token are never retained.
- Personal data is never sent. Only titles, years and provider IDs go to the server.

Build development packages with `python tools/build_packages.py`. Unsigned previews require explicit installation consent; signed publication uses the existing release workflow.

## Compatibility

The plugin reads the contract it declares in its own `manifest.json` (the version the host validates its responses
against) and sends `first_release`, `releases`, game `relations`, the patch `identity`, achievement `aliases` and the `platinum` tier only
when that declaration is 1.1.20 or later. A host older than 1.1.20 refuses to install this release, so it never meets those fields; a build
relabelled to an older contract, or a manifest that cannot be read, sends none of them. An Atlas that has no dates,
keys or platinum yet simply leaves the fields out. Tiers, kinds, crossplay, precisions and release categories are
checked against `vocab.py`, the shared vocabulary of CONTRACTS-v1 C7.4: `contracts/vocab-v1.json` is generated from it
(`python tools/vocab_check.py generate`) and compared with the files Atlas and the host publish (`python
tools/vocab_check.py compare contracts/vocab-v1.json tests/fixtures/atlas/vocab-v1.json
tests/fixtures/host/vocab-v1.json`). Crossplay is `yes`, `partial` or `no`; `not_applicable` is derived by the host and
never sent, and an absent value means unknown. `python tools/check_metadata_atlas_host.py --host-root <host checkout>`
holds the plugin's responses to the host's own validator under both a 1.1.20 and a 1.1.19 declaration.

## Local browser check

For an app and Atlas running in separate Docker containers, set **Atlas API URL** to the container address (for example `http://atlas:8000`) and **Public Atlas URL** to the address your browser can open (for example `http://127.0.0.1:28080`). Save the provider settings, then run **Achievements sync** again under **Settings → Account → Background tasks** so existing achievement icon links are refreshed. The public Atlas URL must serve `/media/<hash>` without requiring a browser token.

This local app test used Atlas 0.7.1 and a small blue icon fixture. The achievement definition, its icon, and separate Pin/Edit controls are visible together:

![Atlas achievement icon loaded in the tracking app](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3105f083-1949-4f8e-9eee-7f7958dd21ab)

## Achievement catalogues

Achievements are read from Atlas in pages (`limit=200`, `offset`, following `next_offset`) and handed to the
host the same way: one Atlas page per response, trimmed to 56 KiB (measured as `json.dumps` of the whole
result) so it stays under the plugin runtime's 64 KiB action output limit. A response that does not fit
returns `next_cursor`, the next unsent Atlas offset, and the host asks again until there is none. Typical
entries are 500 to 800 bytes, so about 70 to 110 fit per response: a 450-entry game takes 5 to 7 responses
and a 2000-entry game about 20 to 30.

Achievement identity: the host `external_id` is the stable `ak1:` key Atlas gives each entry (Atlas contract C2, Atlas
`programme/a4-achievement-identity`), which survives list re-imports, edits and node differences; the Atlas row `id` is
not an identity because older Atlas versions minted a new one on every refresh. The row id travels as
`source_ids["atlas.row"]` so a host that stored the catalogue under row ids can re-key it instead of recreating it.
Against an Atlas without keys the plugin falls back to the row `id` (the previous behaviour). Under Plugin API 1.1.20 an
entry merged from several sources also sends its other keys as `aliases` (at most 32), so the host keeps a stored
definition when the anchor key moves, and Atlas's `platinum` tier is passed through.

The host accepts at most eight `source_ids` per entry. The `atlas.row` bridge takes the first slot, so an entry that
carries eight or more provider ids loses its last provider id(s). The host links catalogue rows to synced platform rows
through `source_ids`, so such an entry can lose that link for the dropped provider; this is a deliberate trade-off to
keep the re-key bridge. Do not ship this plugin version to users before the host re-key (M6) is deployed: until then
the first sync recreates catalogue rows under the new ids, orphans manual-progress overrides and drops media links.
A plugin rollback changes every `external_id` again, so fix forward instead of rolling back.

The host merges the pages by `external_id` (host PR 447), so an entry repeated across a boundary arrives
once. At most 2000 entries are forwarded, and a failed later page is reported as a failure instead of a
truncated list. An Atlas without paging ignores the parameters and returns everything in one response,
which is still split under the byte budget. Atlas paging needs Atlas PR 95
(obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata); without host PR 447 a later page replaces an earlier one.

# HowLongToBeat Metadata Provider

The updated source requires public Plugin API **1.1.13** and the host completion-estimates
update in [host PR #136](https://github.com/Unbound-Timeline-Shelf/Unbound-Timeline-Shelf/pull/136).
It uses no account or API key. Install the corresponding published `.utp` through
Plugin Manager and grant its declared metadata, network and storage permissions.

The provider initializes a short-lived public search token, then searches the
site's current endpoint with browser headers. A search 403 renews the token and
retries once; a second rejection stops. Tokens are not persisted or logged. The
SDK returns 403 directly to the provider instead of multiplying that renewal with
generic background retries. Other failures retain bounded SDK pacing/retry policy.

Metadata returns whichever of Main story, Main + extras, Completionist and All
play styles are available, normalized to one-decimal hours. Missing or invalid
figures are omitted, including when Main story is absent. Existing HLTB identity
wins; without one, only a unique exact normalized title is accepted. Community
estimates never write personal playtime. The host applies manual field protection,
account/provider choices and per-category native IGDB fallback independently.

Build development packages with `python tools/build_packages.py`. Unsigned previews require explicit installation consent; the existing release workflow produces signed publication packages.

Run `python -m pytest tests/test_hltb.py tests/test_metadata_providers.py -q`.
Fixtures cover token renewal bounds, partial/invalid figures, selected identity,
ambiguity and the exported wire schema. A direct public token/search check on
15 October 2026 returned five Portal results; this does not establish installed
package success. Package/runtime integration validation is tracked in the PR.

## Failure behaviour and session handling

No cookie or homepage-visit step is needed: the current flow is the public
`/api/search/site/init` token followed by `/api/search/site`, and the plugin
neither sends nor stores cookies, so no host cookie/session capability is
required. Failures are returned to the host, never swallowed: a retired or failing

# Password Reset

Maintained optional password recovery integration for host Plugin API 1.1.11. This is a functional account flow; the synthetic example remains a separate demonstration.

## Setup

Install the signed official package and explicitly grant the critical **auth.password_reset** permission globally. Open **Administration → Password policy** and find Password recovery below the policy controls. Choose expiry in minutes or hours (10–60 minutes, default 20). **Save settings**, **Enable** and **Disable** are separate controls. Saving disabled settings does not enable recovery; disabling preserves the saved lifetime and invalidates outstanding links. Installation alone does not enable public recovery. The sign-in request and completion flow is unchanged.

Each user must configure an external notification destination, verify it and separately enable recovery delivery. SMTP is built into the host. A plugin destination must declare verification/security/recovery support and hold the independent high-risk provider grant. The authenticated inbox and browser push cannot carry recovery links. Normal routing preferences and administrator restrictions apply; there is no direct SMTP bypass.

## Use

The sign-in page shows **Forgot your password?** when this contribution is active. Request with your app username or configured app email. The acknowledgement is the same for unknown, disabled, SSO and ineligible accounts. Open the delivered link, choose a password satisfying the server policy and confirm. All browser sessions are revoked; **API keys remain active**. Sign in normally afterward.

Links expire, are single-use and are bound to the current account/password/email, installation and configuration revision. Opening a link never consumes it. Bearer material uses a URL fragment and is removed from the displayed address. Disabling/uninstalling or withdrawing the grant blocks pending delivery/redemption; reinstall cannot reclaim old links.

The host stores encrypted delivery material only until consumption/expiry and never puts it in inbox content or lifecycle audit. This plugin stores only its activation/lifetime configuration and never receives reset tokens, passwords, SMTP credentials or account rows.

## Testing

Run `pytest tests/test_official_password_reset.py` and the paired host recovery suite. Actual signed-package installation and the host request/link/redemption workflow are required before release. Temporary SMTP capture is suitable for local acceptance; no production SMTP account is required.

Startup uses auth_flows.password_reset.restore to resume only an already-active matching installation and definition. Withdrawal or reinstallation requires explicit activation; regranting permission cannot revive an old reset credential.

Configuration is under Settings → Administration → Account security → Password recovery. The page shows live **Account recovery enabled/disabled** from the host. Saved preferences do not imply availability. Requires API1.1.10 and explicit settings placement grants. All SMTP mail now uses the host shared HTML design with a plain alternative.

# Unnamed Tracking PWA

The maintained official PWA integrates the mobile repository's PWA assets with
the complete Unnamed Tracking web application. The plugin release version and
the separately reviewed mobile asset version are recorded in
[`manifest.json`](manifest.json) and [`pwa/version.json`](pwa/version.json).
Stable 1.0.0 requires an explicit human release decision.

Install its `.utp` through Plugin Manager, review `frontend.pwa`, and enable it.
The permission publishes public install metadata and icons and enables the
host-owned root worker. It grants no account APIs, native JavaScript or arbitrary
host routes. Only one PWA provider may be enabled per server. The host refuses
conflicting providers rather than selecting one silently.

Use HTTPS (localhost works for development). Android Chrome and Windows
Chrome/Edge offer an install button when available. On iOS Safari, use Share →
Add to Home Screen. Installation requires browser support and is separate from
installing the server plugin. Native Android, WebView and Windows/WinUI clients
remain independent and unchanged.

The installed app opens the full website and uses its normal login/session/SSO.
Passwords are never saved by this plugin. Session expiry returns to normal login.
Offline navigation displays a neutral waiting-for-internet page, never account
data. Private API and authentication responses are never cached. A bounded
exception caches only immutable, digest-addressed public theme assets.
Reconnect restores normal navigation.

The full application, sign-in/SSO redirects and neutral offline page follow
Light, Dark or System and the last device palette, including Orange, Green and
custom colors. Only cosmetic color roles are cached locally; saved account
preferences take precedence online. Browser bars follow the current background.
The public signed installation manifest never contains personal appearance data.

Updates replace the host worker generation and remove only owned old caches.
The offline page has no time expiry. Disable, permission revocation or uninstall
withdraws the manifest/icons and retires the worker when the browser next reaches
the server. Offline devices cannot learn about a server-side removal immediately.
An installed shortcut remains an ordinary website shortcut, with plugin settings
guidance. Reinstallation gets a new installation/cache identity.

Assets are synchronized from [Mobile-Apps/pwa](https://github.com/Unbound-Timeline-Shelf/Mobile-Apps/tree/main/pwa) using
`tools/sync_pwa.py --mobile-root PATH --host-root PATH`; `--check` validates exact
provenance and a plugin release that does not precede its mobile asset version.
The host never executes a worker from an
untrusted package: reviewed worker/offline infrastructure is shipped by the host.
Metadata colors are typed for future theme support; no mobile UI redesign is
included.

Development previews may be unsigned and require explicit untrusted-package
consent. They do not receive the verified Official badge. Official publication
requires a separately registered official public key and protected signing secret.
See [signing configuration](../../docs/official-signing.md).

# User Invites

Maintained official administrator email-invite integration for host Plugin API **1.1.11**.

Configure built-in SMTP in Administration > Notifications. Install this plugin and explicitly approve `auth.user_invites`. Open Administration > Users: User invitations appears below the user controls, and Invite user sits beside Create user. Save settings separately from enabling or disabling invitations. Choose expiry using minutes, hours, days or weeks, within the existing one-hour to one-week bounds (one day by default). Send to the intended recipient email address; do not create an account first.

Email settings include a From display name, subject, heading, welcome message, personal/generic/no greeting, button wording, card/simple layout, accent color and footer. The optional recipient name supplies the personal greeting. A live preview shows the wording and appearance. All content is plain text and escaped by the host. The configured SMTP sender address and host acceptance URL remain authoritative. Wording changes affect future invitations and preserve existing links; lifetime changes and disabling retain credential invalidation behavior. Disabling preserves saved settings. Installation alone does not enable invitations.

The host queues a PRIVATE bootstrap email through the existing notification dispatcher. It uses the configured public app URL, falling back to the issuing administrator's signed-in app address. An allowed secure SMTP transport is required; explicit local-IP/development plaintext exceptions follow the built-in policy. Routing restrictions still apply. The destination exists only for that invitation and cannot receive ordinary or security notices.

The invitee opens the emailed link and chooses a username/password. Opening the link does not consume it. POST acceptance creates an active normal account, never an administrator, and requires normal sign-in afterward. The email address cannot be changed by the acceptance payload. Possession of the invite does not create a verified notification destination automatically.

The administrator page lists the current installation's last 100 invites, expiry and delivery state, and can revoke outstanding links. Sending another invite to the same address retires the earlier link. Requests are bounded to 100 per administrator/day and five per recipient/day, with a global 1,000-row pending capacity. Expired pre-account records are cleaned after a day. Disabling, uninstalling or revoking the grant invalidates old links; reinstall requires explicit activation.

The plugin owns activation and its admin UI. It uses only the public gateway and receives its own invitation email/status records. The host owns tokens, account/password validation, creation, SMTP credentials and delivery retries. Passwords and bearer links never pass through plugin code. Existing registered emails are rejected to the administrator.

This is a usable flow, separate from the synthetic `example.user-invite-notification-demo` routing demonstration.
